newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan 'new' party could spell same old coalition.
newsitem.headline: Japan 'new' party could spell same old coalition.

text.p: A reformist party being patched together with the participation of Japan's popular Health Minister Naoto Kan could grab enough support from disaffected voters to become a partner in a post-election ruling coalition.

But the end result may well be that the party, the latest in a string of new groupings to emerge on Japan's confusing political front, serves mainly as a face-lift that allows the current ruling bloc to stay in power, analysts say.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has yet to set a date for a Lower House election, which is not mandated until next July.

Pundits, however, are betting that Hashimoto, having defused a year-long dispute with Japan's southern island of Okinawa over the heavy concentration of U.S. military bases there, is poised to call an election as early as October 20.

Some LDP leaders say chances of the party winning a majority are slim, so it will again be seeking partners. The ruling bloc now groups the LDP, their one-time rivals in the Social Democratic Party, and the tiny New Party Sakigake.

"The LDP's internal polls show they are not able to win a majority," said Jeff Young, a political analyst at Salomon Brothers Asia. "It may be safe to say even at this point that the new party will hold a swing vote in the next government."

The new Democratic Party, expected to be formally launched closer to election day, has been billed as the brainchild of former Sakigake executive Yukio Hatoyama and his brother Kunio, until recently a member of the main opposition Shinshinto.

The initiative by the two heirs to an elite political family is the latest effort to create a "third political force" as an alternative to Japan's two conservative camps. The brothers want to draw from the Socialists and Sakigake, but baulk at letting old guard leaders from the two parties join.
Fitful talks over who could join combined with what critics complained were "feel good" but fuzzy policies looked set to fritter away political momentum -- until Kan opted to join.

Kan, a Sakigake member, is immensely popular because of his pivotal role in forcing his ministry to accept responsibility for a tainted blood scandal in the 1980s that infected some 1,800 haemophiliacs with the HIV virus, which causes AIDS.

"Kan is a man who has credibility," said political analyst John Neuffer. "The perception is that he's done what no other politician has done in recent times, which is to protect the Japanese people from the bureaucracy."
An opinion poll published on Wednesday by financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun showed that more voters surveyed favoured the Democratic Party than Shinshinto, although the LDP ranked in first place.
The paper said 7.8 percent of those who responded were willing to vote for Democratic Party candidates, 6.5 percent for Shinshinto and 22.4 percent for the LDP.

Political analysts said, however, that the main task for all parties was to attract support from fed-up voters who shun any party allegiance, a description thought to apply to nearly half of all voters.

"The most important fact is that more than 50 percent of the electorate are not in sympathy with any political party," said United Nations University political scientist Takashi Inoguchi. "They are seeking some kind of assurance, hope, excitement...but they could easily get disillusioned."
Many voters have already been disillusioned by the short tenure of the anti-LDP coalition which swept to power in 1993, buoyed by hopes of drastic administrative and economic reform.

"The electorate is jaded about sudden reform parties that come out of nowhere," said Neuffer, adding that the Democratic Party would have an uphill struggle against well-oiled LDP and Shinshinto political machines.
Still, the Democrats could win some 40 to 50 seats and so be well-placed to join an LDP-led coalition -- in effect, yielding the same political lineup now in control.
"An LDP-Democratic Party coalition is the most likely, because it's (the Democratic Party) really the Social Democrats and Sakigake. It's the same, so it's easiest," said Inoguchi.
